lessons.title: The Skeleton: Functions and Structure
lessons.description: Bones of the skeleton, classification by shape and the six functions of the skeleton applied to sport.
lessons.content_html:
Why the Skeleton Matters in Sport

The human skeleton is the rigid framework that makes sport possible. Without it, muscles would have nothing to pull against, vital organs would be unprotected, and the body would have no capacity to produce the forces needed for running, jumping or throwing. Understanding the skeleton — its structure, the shapes of its bones and its six key functions — helps you explain why specific sports place specific demands on specific bones.

The Six Functions of the Skeleton

The skeleton performs six functions that are directly relevant to physical activity and sport.

Protection of vital organs is the most immediately obvious function. The cranium protects the brain; the ribcage — formed by the ribs, sternum and thoracic vertebrae — shields the heart and lungs; the pelvis protects the reproductive organs and bladder. In contact sports such as rugby and boxing, this protective function is critical: the skeleton absorbs and disperses impact forces before they can damage the organs within.

Muscle attachment allows muscles to apply force to bones and produce movement. Muscles do not attach directly to joints — they attach to the surface of bones via tendons. The broader and rougher the bone surface, the greater the area available for muscle attachment. The scapula, for example, provides a large flat surface for the muscles of the shoulder girdle, enabling the wide range of arm movements required in swimming and throwing events.

Joints for movement are formed wherever two or more bones meet. The specific shape of each joint determines which movements are possible. The knee (a hinge joint) allows only flexion and extension, which suits the repetitive straightening action of running. The shoulder (a ball-and-socket joint) allows flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation and circumduction — the full range needed in racket sports and gymnastics.

Key Fact

The six functions of the skeleton are: protection of vital organs, muscle attachment, joints for movement, production of blood cells (red, white and platelets), storage of calcium and phosphorus, and support of the body's shape and posture.

Production of blood cells takes place in the red bone marrow found inside flat and irregular bones such as the sternum, ribs, pelvis and vertebrae. Red blood cells carry oxygen to working muscles; white blood cells fight infection; platelets trigger clotting to stop bleeding after injury. Endurance athletes rely heavily on red blood cell production because greater numbers of red cells means more oxygen can be transported to muscles during prolonged exercise.

Storage of minerals — principally calcium and phosphorus — is another essential function. Bone acts as a mineral bank: when the body needs calcium for muscle contraction or phosphorus for energy metabolism, it can draw on this store. Regular weight-bearing exercise stimulates bones to increase their mineral density, reducing the risk of stress fractures in athletes.

Support is the structural function that allows the body to stand upright and maintain posture during activity. The vertebral column supports the entire weight of the upper body and transmits force between the lower limbs and the trunk. In events like weightlifting and gymnastics, maintaining correct spinal alignment is critical to both performance and injury prevention.

Classification of Bones by Shape

Bones are grouped into five categories based on their shape. Each category has a function that reflects its form.

Long bones are the levers of the body. Examples include the femur (upper leg), humerus (upper arm), tibia, fibula, radius and ulna. Their length gives muscles a mechanical advantage, so a small amount of muscle shortening at one end produces a large arc of movement at the other. Sprinters depend on long femurs to generate stride length; throwers rely on a long humerus to generate club-head speed.

Short bones are roughly cube-shaped and are built for weight-bearing and shock absorption rather than movement. The carpals of the wrist and the tarsals of the ankle are short bones. They allow the small, precise adjustments of wrist and ankle position needed in gymnastics and ballet without sacrificing stability.

Flat bones are thin, plate-like structures. Examples include the skull (cranium), the scapula, the ribs and the sternum. Their large surface area makes them ideal for muscle attachment as well as organ protection. The pectoralis major, for instance, attaches broadly to the sternum and clavicle, generating the powerful pushing force used in a swimming butterfly stroke.

Irregular bones have complex shapes that do not fit the other categories. The vertebrae are the primary example: their irregular shape allows them to lock together to protect the spinal cord while also providing attachment points for the deep muscles of the back. The bones of the face are also irregular.

Sesamoid bones are a fifth category that Edexcel specifically requires. They develop inside tendons where those tendons cross a joint and are subjected to compression. The patella (kneecap) is the most important example. It sits inside the quadriceps tendon as it crosses the front of the knee, protecting the tendon from wear and increasing the mechanical advantage of the quadriceps muscle when straightening the knee — useful in every kicking and jumping action in sport.

Key Fact

Edexcel requires five bone shape categories: long (e.g. femur — leverage), short (e.g. carpals — weight-bearing), flat (e.g. scapula — protection and muscle attachment), irregular (e.g. vertebrae — protection and muscle attachment), and sesamoid (e.g. patella — embedded in tendons to improve leverage). AQA only teaches four categories; make sure you include sesamoid.

Key Bones of the Skeleton

You need to know the location and classification of these bones: cranium, clavicle, scapula, the five regions of the vertebral column (cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacrum, coccyx), ribs, sternum, humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges (hand), pelvis, femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals and phalanges (foot).

Working down from the head: the cranium is a flat bone protecting the brain. The clavicle (collar bone) and scapula (shoulder blade) are flat bones of the shoulder girdle. The vertebral column consists of 33 irregular bones in five regions — 7 cervical (neck), 12 thoracic (mid-back, each attached to a rib), 5 lumbar (lower back), fused sacrum and fused coccyx. The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm; the radius and ulna are the long bones of the forearm. The carpals are the short bones of the wrist; the metacarpals and phalanges form the hand and fingers.

In the lower body, the pelvis is an irregular bone that connects the spine to the legs and protects abdominal organs. The femur is the longest bone in the body — a long bone that runs from hip to knee. The patella sits at the front of the knee as a sesamoid bone. The tibia (shin) and fibula are the long bones of the lower leg. The tarsals are the short bones of the ankle; the metatarsals and phalanges form the foot and toes.

Students often classify the patella as a flat bone because it looks flat and plate-like. The Edexcel mark scheme classifies it as a sesamoid bone because it developed inside a tendon — the quadriceps tendon. The distinguishing feature of a sesamoid bone is not its shape but its origin: it forms within soft tissue (a tendon or ligament) rather than from a separate centre of ossification. In the exam, if asked to classify the patella, always write “sesamoid” and explain that it is embedded within the quadriceps tendon.

When you place a mechanical load on a bone during weight-bearing exercise — running, jumping, weightlifting — the bone responds by depositing more calcium and phosphorus into its matrix, increasing bone density. This is a long-term training adaptation. Conversely, inactivity or zero-gravity environments cause bones to lose mineral density, weakening them. For athletes, this is why cross-training with weight-bearing activity matters even for swimmers and cyclists whose main sport is non-impact.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In questions asking you to “classify” a bone, name the shape category and give the functional reason — for example, “The femur is a long bone; its length acts as a lever to transmit muscular force into movement.” For the patella, always write “sesamoid” — not flat. On Identify questions, commit to one answer: if you write two conflicting classifications, the mark scheme takes the first answer given, which may be the wrong one. On 6-mark Analyse questions about the skeleton, structure your answer by linking function → bone shape → sporting example (e.g. protection → cranium is flat → helmets supplement it in cycling).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The skeleton has six functions applied to sport: protection, muscle attachment, joints for movement, blood cell production, mineral storage and support — each function links directly to performance demands.
  • Bones are classified into five shapes: long (leverage), short (weight-bearing), flat (protection/muscle attachment), irregular (protection/muscle attachment) and sesamoid (embedded in tendons — e.g. the patella).
  • Knowing the location and classification of each named bone allows you to answer context questions about why specific injuries, movements or training adaptations occur at specific sites.

lessons.title: Joints, Ligaments and Tendons
lessons.description: Types of synovial joint, the movements they allow and how ligaments and tendons enable safe movement.
lessons.content_html:
Joints: Where Movement Happens

A joint is any point where two or more bones meet. The type of joint determines precisely which movements are possible at that site. For GCSE Physical Education, you need to know four types of synovial joint — pivot, hinge, condyloid and ball-and-socket — and for each type: where it is in the body, which movements it permits, and how those movements appear in sport.

The Four Synovial Joint Types

All four joint types share the same basic synovial structure: a fluid-filled cavity enclosed in a fibrous capsule, with cartilage covering the bone surfaces to reduce friction. What differs is the shape of the articulating surfaces, which determines the range of permitted movement.

The pivot joint permits rotation only. The two pivot joints in the body are the atlanto-axial joint (between the atlas and axis — the top two cervical vertebrae), which allows you to rotate your head side-to-side as in a swimmer checking for a lane marker, and the proximal radioulnar joint in the forearm, which allows pronation and supination of the palm — movements used in badminton smashes and cricket spin bowling.

The hinge joint works like a door hinge, permitting flexion and extension in a single plane. The three hinge joints relevant to sport are the elbow (humerus and ulna), the knee (femur and tibia) and the ankle (tibia/fibula and talus). The knee produces the powerful extension needed to drive off the ground in sprinting; the ankle hinge is the axis for plantar-flexion (pointing the foot, as when a gymnast points their toes) and dorsi-flexion (lifting the toes, as when pulling the foot up at the end of each stride).

The condyloid joint (sometimes called an ellipsoidal joint) allows movement in two planes: flexion and extension plus abduction and adduction, giving circumduction but not rotation. The primary example is the wrist (radius and carpals). The condyloid joint at the base of each finger (metacarpophalangeal joints) also belongs to this category. In sport, the wrist condyloid joint allows the flicking motion used in a basketball free throw and the angling of the wrist in catching a cricket ball.

Key Fact

The four synovial joint types: pivot (atlanto-axial, radioulnar — rotation only), hinge (elbow, knee, ankle — flexion/extension), condyloid (wrist — flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction), ball-and-socket (hip, shoulder — all movements including rotation and circumduction).

The ball-and-socket joint is the most mobile joint in the body, allowing movement in all planes. The shoulder (humerus head into the glenoid cavity of the scapula) and the hip (femur head into the acetabulum of the pelvis) are ball-and-socket joints. The shoulder allows the greatest range, including the full-arm circumduction used in freestyle swimming and the overarm throwing action in cricket. The hip allows the wide abduction needed in a gymnastics box split and the powerful extension that drives each running stride.

Movements at Joints

You need to know nine specific movement terms and apply them to sporting actions. Flexion is decreasing the angle at a joint — bending the elbow to bring the hand towards the shoulder. Extension is increasing the angle — straightening the elbow when pushing in a press-up. Abduction is moving a limb away from the midline of the body — raising the arm sideways in a jumping jack. Adduction is moving towards the midline — lowering the arm back to the side. Rotation is turning a bone around its own long axis — the internal rotation of the humerus in a forehand tennis stroke. Circumduction is a combined cone-shaped movement combining flexion, extension, abduction and adduction — the arm action of a windmill bowling in cricket. Plantar-flexion is pointing the foot downward at the ankle — pushing off the floor in a sprint start. Dorsi-flexion is pulling the foot upward at the ankle — the heel-strike phase of running.

Students often confuse condyloid and ball-and-socket joints because both allow circumduction. The key difference is rotation: a ball-and-socket joint allows rotation of the limb around its long axis; a condyloid joint does not. Try rotating your wrist like a screwdriver — that movement actually comes from the radioulnar pivot joint, not the wrist condyloid joint. The wrist itself only flexes, extends, abducts and adducts. The shoulder, by contrast, can rotate the humerus independently of any other movement — as when winding up a throw. In exam questions, if asked whether the wrist allows rotation, the answer is no.

Ligaments and Tendons

Ligaments connect bone to bone. They are made of dense, fibrous connective tissue that is flexible enough to allow normal joint movement but strong enough to prevent the joint from dislocating or moving beyond its safe range. The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) of the knee, for example, prevents the tibia from sliding forward on the femur — it is commonly ruptured in football and skiing when the knee twists under load.

Tendons connect muscle to bone. They transmit the contractile force generated by the muscle belly to the bone, causing the bone to move at the joint. Tendons are inelastic — they do not stretch under load the way muscles do. The Achilles tendon connects the gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus (heel bone) and is the largest tendon in the body, transmitting the enormous forces generated during jumping and sprinting. Tendons can become inflamed (tendinopathy) from repetitive overuse.

Key Fact

Ligaments connect bone to bone, stabilising joints. Tendons connect muscle to bone, transmitting the pull of muscle to create movement. Ligaments are most at risk in contact and twisting sports (e.g. ACL in football); tendons are most at risk in repetitive overuse activities (e.g. Achilles tendinopathy in distance running).

Ligaments have a relatively poor blood supply compared to muscles. When a ligament is sprained — stretched or partially torn — the limited blood flow means the repair process is slow. Partial tears may take 6–12 weeks to heal; complete tears (rupture) of major ligaments such as the ACL often require surgical reconstruction followed by months of rehabilitation. This is why protecting ligaments through correct technique, appropriate footwear and gradual progressive overload is a key principle of sports injury prevention. Good proprioceptive training (balance work) also strengthens the neural reflexes that prevent joints from entering unsafe ranges in the first place.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A very common mistake is confusing ligaments and tendons. Remember: Ligament links Bone to Bone; Tendon connects to Bone from Muscle. On Describe questions about joints, always name the joint type, the bones involved, and at least two movements it allows — partial answers that name the type but omit movements lose marks. On the pivot joint, make sure you name the specific location (atlanto-axial or radioulnar) and state rotation as the only permitted movement. On 4-mark Discuss questions comparing joint types, aim for ‘On one hand… on the other hand…’ with a sporting example for each type.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • There are four synovial joint types: pivot (rotation only — neck/radioulnar), hinge (flexion/extension — elbow, knee, ankle), condyloid (flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction — wrist), and ball-and-socket (all movements — hip, shoulder).
  • Nine movement terms apply to joints: flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, circumduction, plantar-flexion, dorsi-flexion — each linked to specific sporting actions.
  • Ligaments connect bone to bone, stabilising joints; tendons connect muscle to bone, transmitting force. Both are at risk of injury in sport — sprains (ligament) and tendinopathy (tendon) are among the most common sporting injuries.

lessons.title: Muscle Types and Major Muscles
lessons.description: Voluntary, involuntary and cardiac muscle, and the location and role of the major skeletal muscles.
lessons.content_html:
Three Types of Muscle

The body contains three distinct types of muscle tissue, and understanding how they differ explains why the heart never tires, why you cannot choose to stop digesting food, and why a trained sprinter can consciously contract the quadriceps with explosive force. Each muscle type has a structure suited to its role.

Voluntary (skeletal) muscle is attached to bones via tendons and is under your conscious control. You decide to kick a football, and the voluntary muscles of your leg contract to do it. Skeletal muscle is striated — it appears striped under a microscope because of the alternating light and dark bands of the protein filaments that generate force. Voluntary muscles fatigue over time and need rest to recover. All 12 muscles you need to know for this specification are voluntary muscles.

Involuntary (smooth) muscle is found in the walls of blood vessels, the digestive tract and other hollow organs. It is not under conscious control — it contracts automatically in response to signals from the autonomic nervous system and hormones. Its contractions are slower and sustained. In sport, the involuntary muscle in the walls of arterioles controls vasoconstriction and vasodilation to redirect blood to working muscles during exercise.

Cardiac muscle forms the walls of the heart. Like smooth muscle it is involuntary; like skeletal muscle it is striated. It is unique because it contracts rhythmically and automatically (intrinsic rhythmicity) without needing external nerve signals, though the autonomic nervous system can speed it up or slow it down. Cardiac muscle is highly resistant to fatigue — it must beat approximately 100,000 times per day for a lifetime without resting. Its cells are interconnected so that electrical signals spread instantly across the whole heart wall, producing a coordinated, powerful contraction.

Key Fact

Three muscle types: voluntary (skeletal) — attached to bones, conscious control, produces joint movement; involuntary (smooth) — blood vessel walls, automatic, controls blood distribution; cardiac — heart wall, involuntary but striated, never fatigues, maintains circulation throughout exercise.

The 12 Major Voluntary Muscles

You need to know the location and sporting function of twelve skeletal muscles. Work through them from the upper body downwards.

The deltoid caps the shoulder. It is the prime mover for arm abduction (raising the arm sideways), as seen when a swimmer pulls the arm out to the side in a butterfly stroke or when a basketball player passes overhead. The biceps (front of the upper arm) flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm — essential in every pulling movement in sport, from rowing to rock climbing. The triceps (back of the upper arm) extends the elbow — it drives the arm-straightening phase of a push-up, a javelin throw and a handball shot.

The pectoralis major lies across the front of the chest. It adducts and medially rotates the humerus, generating the sweeping arm movement in butterfly swimming and the chest-pass in basketball. The latissimus dorsi (“lats”) spans the back from the lower spine to the humerus. It extends and adducts the arm — responsible for the powerful downward pull in swimming and the pulling phase in rowing. The external obliques run diagonally down the sides of the abdomen and rotate the trunk, crucial for throwing, striking and changing direction at speed.

The hip flexors (including the iliopsoas group) flex the hip joint, swinging the thigh forward in every running stride. The gluteus maximus extends the hip — it is the largest muscle in the body and drives the backward push of each stride, the power phase of a squat and the jump in volleyball.

The quadriceps (four muscles at the front of the thigh) extend the knee. They straighten the leg in kicking, jumping and the final push of a sprint. The hamstrings (three muscles at the back of the thigh) flex the knee and assist hip extension. They decelerate the swinging leg in sprinting and are among the most commonly strained muscles in sport.

The gastrocnemius is the large calf muscle that crosses both the knee and ankle joints. It plantar-flexes the ankle — pointing the foot downward in a sprint start or ballet rise. It also assists knee flexion. The tibialis anterior runs down the front of the shin and dorsi-flexes the ankle, lifting the toes during the swing phase of running and ensuring the heel strikes the ground cleanly.

Key Fact

The 12 major muscles you must know: deltoid (shoulder abduction), biceps (elbow flexion), triceps (elbow extension), pectoralis major (arm adduction/rotation), latissimus dorsi (arm extension/adduction), external obliques (trunk rotation), hip flexors (hip flexion), gluteus maximus (hip extension), quadriceps (knee extension), hamstrings (knee flexion/hip extension), gastrocnemius (plantar-flexion), tibialis anterior (dorsi-flexion).

Both cardiac and smooth muscle are involuntary, but they are structurally different. Cardiac muscle is striated (like skeletal muscle) because it contains the same overlapping actin-myosin filament arrangement needed to generate high force quickly. Smooth muscle is non-striated — its filaments are arranged in a less regular pattern, producing slower, more sustained contractions appropriate for maintaining blood vessel tone and moving food through the gut. In the exam, if asked to state one difference between cardiac and smooth muscle, the key answer is: cardiac is striated and contracts with high force; smooth is non-striated and contracts more slowly.

Taking a football kick as an example: the hip flexors contract to swing the thigh forward (hip flexion at the ball-and-socket hip joint). As the foot approaches the ball, the quadriceps contract powerfully to extend the knee (hinge joint), while the gastrocnemius plantar-flexes the ankle to point the foot for contact. The tibialis anterior relaxes to allow plantar-flexion. At the same time, the external obliques rotate the trunk to add rotational power. The bones of the leg — femur, tibia, fibula — act as levers, amplifying the force generated by each muscle. This is the musculo-skeletal system in action: muscles provide force; bones provide the rigid lever; joints provide the pivot points.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions that ask you to ‘state the location and role’ of a muscle expect both pieces of information — location alone, or action alone, will only score one mark of two. Use precise anatomical language: ‘the quadriceps are located at the front of the thigh and extend the knee joint’ is a full two-mark answer. On 3-mark Explain questions linking muscle to movement, use the structure: muscle name → contraction type → joint action → sporting example. On 6-mark Assess questions about the musculo-skeletal system, refer to at least three named muscles and link each to a specific movement in a named sport to demonstrate application.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Three muscle types: voluntary (skeletal) — conscious control, produces joint movement; involuntary (smooth) — blood vessel walls, automatic; cardiac — heart wall, involuntary but striated, never fatigues.
  • The 12 major muscles span the body from the deltoid at the shoulder to the tibialis anterior at the shin — each has a named location and a specific joint action relevant to sport.
  • The muscular and skeletal systems work together: muscles generate force, bones transmit it as levers, and joints provide the pivot points for movement in physical activity.

lessons.title: Antagonistic Pairs and Muscle Fibre Types
lessons.description: Agonist and antagonist roles in sporting actions and how slow and fast twitch fibres suit different activities.
lessons.content_html:
Muscles Work in Opposing Pairs

Muscles can only pull — they cannot push. To produce movement in one direction and then reverse it, muscles work in opposing pairs called antagonistic pairs. In every movement, one muscle contracts to produce the movement (the agonist) while the opposing muscle relaxes and lengthens to allow it (the antagonist).

The roles of agonist and antagonist swap when the movement is reversed. At the elbow: during a bicep curl (elbow flexion) the biceps is the agonist and the triceps is the antagonist. When you straighten your arm back down (elbow extension) the triceps becomes the agonist and the biceps becomes the antagonist. This reciprocal relationship is how smooth, controlled movement is produced.

The Four Key Antagonistic Pairs

You need to know four antagonistic pairs with their specific joint actions.

Biceps and triceps at the elbow: The biceps flexes the elbow (agonist in a rowing pull, a pull-up, a forehand shot in badminton) while the triceps relaxes. To extend the elbow (shot put release, press-up push, javelin throw) the triceps becomes the agonist and the biceps relaxes.

Quadriceps and hamstrings at the knee: The quadriceps extend the knee (agonist in kicking, jumping, the push phase of cycling) while the hamstrings relax. To flex the knee (recovery leg in sprinting, curling the leg in swimming breaststroke kick) the hamstrings become the agonist and the quadriceps relax. The hamstrings are particularly prone to strain when they contract rapidly as the agonist during the late swing phase of sprinting — when they decelerate the extending knee.

Hip flexors and gluteus maximus at the hip: The hip flexors flex the hip (agonist when swinging the leg forward in running) while the gluteus maximus relaxes. When the hip extends — the drive phase pushing the leg backward in running, the downstroke in cycling, the jump in volleyball — the gluteus maximus is the agonist and the hip flexors relax.

Gastrocnemius and tibialis anterior at the ankle: The gastrocnemius plantar-flexes the ankle (agonist in a sprint start, a jump take-off, pointing the foot in gymnastics) while the tibialis anterior relaxes. When dorsi-flexion is needed (heel-strike landing, pulling the foot up in the swing phase of running) the tibialis anterior is the agonist and the gastrocnemius relaxes.

Key Fact

Four antagonistic pairs and their joints: biceps/triceps (elbow), quadriceps/hamstrings (knee), hip flexors/gluteus maximus (hip), gastrocnemius/tibialis anterior (ankle). In each case, the agonist contracts and the antagonist relaxes; roles swap when movement direction reverses.

Students often assume the agonist must always be the bigger, stronger muscle. This is wrong — the agonist is simply whichever muscle is producing the current movement. The tibialis anterior is smaller than the gastrocnemius, but when you dorsi-flex the ankle (pull the foot up) the tibialis anterior is the agonist and the gastrocnemius is the antagonist, regardless of their relative sizes. The key is to anchor your answer to the specific phase of movement described in the question. Exam questions often ask “identify the agonist during the upward phase of a bicep curl” or “name the antagonist when the knee is being extended.” Always start by identifying the movement phase, then name the muscle contracting to produce it as the agonist.

Muscle Fibre Types

Not all muscle fibres are the same. Skeletal muscles contain a mixture of three fibre types with very different properties, and the proportion of each type influences which activities a performer is naturally suited to.

Type I fibres (slow-twitch) contract slowly but are highly resistant to fatigue. They have a rich blood supply, many mitochondria and high levels of myoglobin (the protein that stores oxygen in muscle), which gives them a red colour. They generate force aerobically and can sustain activity for long periods. Marathon runners and professional cyclists have a high proportion of Type I fibres, and activities like long-distance swimming, cross-country running and triathlon rely on them heavily.

Type IIa fibres (fast-twitch oxidative) represent an intermediate option. They contract faster than Type I fibres and produce more force, but they can also use aerobic metabolism when required. They fatigue more quickly than Type I but more slowly than Type IIx. They are dominant in activities requiring a sustained but high effort — 400 m and 800 m running, many team sports such as football and rugby where repeated bursts are interspersed with recovery periods.

Type IIx fibres (fast-twitch glycolytic) are the fastest and most powerful but fatigue very rapidly. They rely almost entirely on anaerobic energy sources (glycogen, phosphocreatine) and have few mitochondria. They are activated only for maximal-intensity, short-duration efforts: 100 m sprinting, shot put, Olympic weightlifting, plyometric jumping. Sprinters like Dina Asher-Smith have a genetic advantage in Type IIx fibre proportion, which contributes to explosive acceleration.

Key Fact

Three fibre types: Type I (slow-twitch, aerobic, fatigue-resistant — marathon); Type IIa (intermediate, aerobic and anaerobic, moderate fatigue — 800 m / team sports); Type IIx (fast-twitch, anaerobic, rapid fatigue — 100 m sprint / weightlifting).

Research suggests that the ratio of Type I to Type II fibres is largely determined by genetics and does not change significantly with training. However, there is some evidence that Type IIx fibres can be converted to Type IIa fibres with prolonged aerobic training, and that resistance training can increase the size (hypertrophy) of both Type II subtypes, increasing their force output. For GCSE purposes, the key point is: fibre type is genetically determined (you choose your parents wisely if you want to be a sprinter), but fibre size and efficiency can be improved through appropriate training. This is why elite sprinters and elite endurance athletes have very different physiological profiles.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On questions about antagonistic pairs, always anchor your answer to the specific phase of movement — ‘during elbow flexion’ or ‘during the upward phase.’ The mark scheme distinguishes agonist and antagonist by movement phase, not by anatomy alone. On muscle fibre questions, use the full Edexcel labels: Type I, Type IIa, Type IIx — do not write ‘slow-twitch’ or ‘fast-twitch’ alone as these are informal descriptors. Justify your sport–fibre match with a reason: ‘Type I because the marathon is a prolonged aerobic activity lasting over two hours, requiring fatigue-resistant fibres’ scores more marks than naming the type alone.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • In antagonistic pairs, the agonist contracts to produce a movement while the antagonist relaxes; the four key pairs are biceps/triceps (elbow), quadriceps/hamstrings (knee), hip flexors/gluteus maximus (hip), gastrocnemius/tibialis anterior (ankle).
  • Three muscle fibre types: Type I (slow-twitch, aerobic, endurance), Type IIa (intermediate, aerobic and anaerobic, team sports), Type IIx (fast-twitch, anaerobic, explosive power).
  • The proportion of fibre types is largely genetically determined and influences athletic suitability; training can improve fibre size and efficiency but cannot fundamentally alter the ratio of slow to fast fibres.

lessons.title: The Cardiovascular System and Exercise
lessons.description: Heart structure, the pathway of blood and how the cardiovascular system responds to physical activity.
lessons.content_html:
The Heart and Blood: Delivering Oxygen to Working Muscles

The cardiovascular system is the body’s transport network. It delivers oxygen and nutrients to every working cell and removes waste products including carbon dioxide and heat. During exercise, the demand for oxygen in the muscles multiplies, and the cardiovascular system responds with a series of rapid adjustments to maintain performance. Understanding these structures and responses is central to this topic.

Functions of the Cardiovascular System

The cardiovascular system has four key functions in physical activity. First, transport of oxygen: red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to working muscles, enabling aerobic energy production. Second, transport of carbon dioxide: blood carries CO2 away from muscles back to the lungs for exhalation. Third, transport of nutrients: glucose and fatty acids travel in the plasma to fuel muscle contractions. Fourth, regulation of body temperature: blood carries heat from working muscles to the skin surface, where it can be dissipated through sweating and radiation.

Additionally, blood contributes to clotting of open wounds via platelets — protecting athletes from blood loss after contact injuries — and to immune defence via white blood cells.

Structure of the Heart

The heart is a double pump, divided into left and right sides by the septum. Each side has an upper chamber (an atrium) and a lower chamber (a ventricle). The right side deals with deoxygenated blood; the left side deals with oxygenated blood.

Blood flows through the heart in a precise sequence. Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium via the vena cava (the large vein returning blood from the upper and lower body). It passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. From there it is pumped out through the pulmonary artery to the lungs to pick up oxygen. Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs via the pulmonary vein into the left atrium. It passes through the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the left ventricle, which pumps it out through the aorta to the rest of the body.

The semi-lunar valves sit at the exits of both ventricles — one at the base of the pulmonary artery (pulmonary semi-lunar valve) and one at the base of the aorta (aortic semi-lunar valve). Their job is to prevent blood flowing back into the ventricles after each contraction. The “lub-dub” sound of the heartbeat is the sound of these valves — and the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and bicuspid) — snapping shut.

Key Fact

Blood pathway through the heart: vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid valve → left ventricle → aorta → body.

Blood Vessels: Arteries, Capillaries and Veins

Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure. Their thick, muscular and elastic walls withstand and smooth out the surges of pressure produced by each heartbeat. The aorta is the largest artery, branching into progressively smaller arteries as it distributes blood to all regions of the body.

Capillaries are the smallest vessels, with walls only one cell thick. This ultra-thin wall allows oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide to diffuse freely between the blood and the muscle fibres. A dense network of capillaries surrounds every active muscle fibre, and endurance training increases the density of this network — one of the key long-term adaptations covered in Lesson 9.

Veins return blood to the heart under low pressure. Their walls are thinner than arteries because the pressure is much lower. Veins contain valves that prevent blood from flowing backwards (particularly important in the legs where blood must travel upward against gravity).

Cardiac Output, Stroke Volume and Heart Rate

Cardiac output (Q) is the total amount of blood pumped by the heart per minute. It is calculated by the formula:

$$Q = \text{stroke volume} \times \text{heart rate}$$

Stroke volume (SV) is the amount of blood pumped out with each beat. At rest a typical adult has a stroke volume of around 70 ml. Heart rate (HR) at rest is typically 60–80 bpm. So resting cardiac output is approximately 70 × 70 = 4,900 ml/min (roughly 5 litres per minute).

During maximal exercise, heart rate can reach 200 bpm and stroke volume can increase to 110–130 ml in a fit person, giving a cardiac output of over 20 litres per minute — a four-fold increase. This increased delivery of oxygenated blood to muscles is the central cardiovascular response to exercise.

Key Fact

Cardiac output (Q) = stroke volume (SV) × heart rate (HR). At rest: ~70 ml × 70 bpm = ~4,900 ml/min. During maximal exercise: cardiac output can exceed 20,000 ml/min (20 L/min) as both SV and HR increase.

Vascular shunting is the process by which blood is redirected during exercise. At rest, organs such as the gut, liver and kidneys receive a large proportion of cardiac output. During intense exercise, the arterioles supplying these organs vasoconstrict (their smooth muscle contracts, narrowing the vessel), while the arterioles supplying the working muscles vasodilate (relax and widen), directing a much greater fraction of cardiac output to the muscles that need it. This redistribution can shift up to 80% of cardiac output to working muscles during maximal exercise, compared with around 15–20% at rest.

Blood is a mixture of cells and fluid. Red blood cells (erythrocytes) contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the muscles. They have no nucleus, maximising their oxygen-carrying capacity. White blood cells (leucocytes) form part of the immune system, destroying pathogens. Platelets (thrombocytes) trigger blood clotting when a vessel is damaged. Plasma is the fluid component (about 55% of blood volume) that transports cells, dissolved gases, nutrients, hormones and waste products. Plasma also distributes heat generated by working muscles to the skin for cooling.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Calculation questions on cardiac output follow a simple two-step pattern: (1) write the formula, Q = SV × HR; (2) substitute the values; (3) state the answer with units (ml/min or L/min). Always include units — the mark scheme requires them. On Explain questions about exercise responses, use the ‘what changes → why → so that’ chain: ‘heart rate increases (what) because the sympathetic nervous system sends signals to the sinoatrial node (why), so that more oxygen-rich blood reaches working muscles (so that).’ On valve questions, remember: tricuspid is on the right, bicuspid on the left. A useful memory aid: bicuspid has two flaps and is on the left side — two letters in ‘left’, two flaps.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The heart is a four-chambered double pump: right side moves deoxygenated blood to the lungs; left side moves oxygenated blood to the body. Blood flows through in the sequence: vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid → left ventricle → aorta.
  • Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. At rest, around 5 L/min; during maximal exercise, over 20 L/min — driven by increases in both stroke volume and heart rate.
  • Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; capillaries are the site of gas and nutrient exchange; veins return blood to the heart under low pressure. Vascular shunting redirects blood to working muscles during exercise.

lessons.title: The Respiratory System and Gas Exchange
lessons.description: The pathway of air, breathing mechanics and how gas exchange in the alveoli supports activity.
lessons.content_html:
Breathing and Gas Exchange

Every sporting action requires energy, and most energy for sustained activity comes from aerobic respiration, which demands a continuous supply of oxygen and an efficient means of removing carbon dioxide. The respiratory system provides both. It moves air in and out of the body, extracts oxygen from inhaled air and expels the CO2 produced by working muscles. Understanding the pathway of air, the mechanics of breathing and the process of gas exchange at the alveoli underpins everything else in applied anatomy and physiology.

The Pathway of Air

Air enters through the nose or mouth and travels down the trachea (windpipe) into the chest. The trachea divides into two bronchi (singular: bronchus), one entering each lung. Inside the lungs, each bronchus branches repeatedly into smaller and smaller airways called bronchioles. At the end of each bronchiole sits a cluster of tiny air sacs called alveoli (singular: alveolus). It is here, at the alveoli, that oxygen passes into the bloodstream and carbon dioxide passes out.

The diaphragm is the primary muscle of breathing. It sits below the lungs as a dome-shaped sheet of muscle. The external intercostal muscles run between the ribs and assist breathing by raising the ribcage. Together, these structures create the pressure changes that move air in and out.

Breathing Mechanics

During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens downward, while the external intercostal muscles contract and lift the ribcage upward and outward. This increases the volume of the thoracic (chest) cavity, reducing the air pressure inside. Air rushes in down the pressure gradient from the higher-pressure atmosphere into the lower-pressure lungs.

During exhalation at rest, the diaphragm and external intercostals relax. The elastic recoil of the lung tissue and the weight of the ribcage cause the thoracic volume to decrease, pressure rises above atmospheric, and air is pushed out. During exercise, when faster and deeper breathing is needed, the internal intercostal muscles and abdominal muscles actively assist exhalation by compressing the thoracic cavity further.

Tidal Volume and Vital Capacity

Tidal volume is the amount of air moved per breath. At rest, a typical adult’s tidal volume is about 0.5 litres. During maximal exercise, tidal volume can rise to around 3 litres as the body demands more oxygen. This increase is due to the deeper contractions of the diaphragm and the active engagement of the intercostal and abdominal muscles.

Vital capacity is the maximum amount of air that can be exhaled after a maximal inhalation. It is used as a measure of lung capacity and typically ranges from 3 to 6 litres depending on body size, sex and training status. Endurance athletes tend to have higher vital capacities than untrained individuals, partly due to strengthening of the respiratory muscles and increased chest wall flexibility. Regular aerobic training can modestly increase vital capacity over time.

Key Fact

Air pathway: nose/mouth → trachea → bronchi (one per lung) → bronchioles → alveoli. At the alveoli: O2 diffuses into blood; CO2 diffuses out. Tidal volume rises from ~0.5 L at rest to ~3 L during maximal exercise. Vital capacity is the maximum air exhaled after a full breath in.

Gas Exchange at the Alveoli

Gas exchange works by diffusion — gases move from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration across a thin membrane. The alveoli are designed to maximise the rate of diffusion. Each alveolus is surrounded by a dense network of pulmonary capillaries. The combined wall of the alveolus and the capillary is only two cells thick, providing the shortest possible diffusion distance.

Inhaled air is richer in oxygen (about 21%) than the deoxygenated blood arriving from the working muscles (which has used most of its oxygen). Oxygen therefore diffuses from the alveolar air into the blood. Carbon dioxide concentration is higher in the blood (produced by aerobic respiration in the muscles) than in the alveolar air, so CO2 diffuses from the blood into the alveolus to be exhaled. This simultaneous exchange happens continuously — as long as you are breathing and your heart is beating.

Inhaled air contains approximately 21% oxygen and 0.04% CO2. Exhaled air contains approximately 16% oxygen and 4% CO2, reflecting the oxygen taken up and the CO2 expelled. The nitrogen content (~78%) is virtually unchanged because the body neither uses nor produces it.

Key Fact

Inhaled vs exhaled air: O2 falls from ~21% to ~16%; CO2 rises from ~0.04% to ~4%. This difference reflects the oxygen absorbed and CO2 produced by working tissues. At the alveoli, diffusion is maximised by: large surface area, thin membrane, rich blood supply and steep concentration gradients maintained by breathing and circulation.

The respiratory and cardiovascular systems must operate in synchrony. Oxygen absorbed at the alveoli immediately enters the pulmonary capillaries and is carried by haemoglobin in red blood cells via the pulmonary vein to the left side of the heart. From there, the left ventricle pumps it out through the aorta to the working muscles. At the muscle capillaries, oxygen diffuses from the blood into the muscle fibres while CO2 diffuses from the fibres into the blood. The blood, now deoxygenated and CO2-rich, returns via the vena cava to the right side of the heart, is pumped to the lungs, and the cycle repeats. During intense exercise, both systems up-regulate together: breathing rate and depth increase to bring more O2 to the alveoli; heart rate and stroke volume increase to transport it faster. If either system is limited (e.g. by asthma reducing airflow, or anaemia reducing haemoglobin), exercise capacity is compromised.

During maximal, short-duration anaerobic exercise (e.g. a 100 m sprint), the demand for oxygen exceeds what the cardiovascular and respiratory systems can deliver. Muscles shift to anaerobic respiration and accumulate lactic acid. The lungs are still exchanging gases as fast as possible, but the limiting factor is the delivery rate, not the exchange mechanism itself. After the sprint, breathing rate remains elevated to repay the oxygen debt (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption, EPOC) — the extra oxygen needed to remove lactic acid and restore the body’s pre-exercise state.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining gas exchange, use the word ‘diffusion’ and state the direction of movement for each gas (O2 into blood, CO2 out of blood) with the reason (concentration gradient). Merely writing ‘oxygen goes into the blood and CO2 comes out’ without the mechanism scores only partial credit. On 2-mark Describe questions about breathing, distinguish between the action of the diaphragm (contracts and flattens during inhalation) and the intercostals (lift the ribcage) — naming one but not the other loses a mark. For tidal volume and vital capacity questions, use precise units (litres, L) in your answer.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Air travels: nose/mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. At the alveoli, O2 diffuses into the blood and CO2 diffuses out, driven by concentration gradients.
  • Inhalation: diaphragm contracts (flattens), external intercostals raise the ribcage, thoracic volume increases, pressure drops, air rushes in. Tidal volume rises from ~0.5 L at rest to ~3 L during maximal exercise.
  • Inhaled air is ~21% O2 / ~0.04% CO2; exhaled air is ~16% O2 / ~4% CO2. The respiratory and cardiovascular systems work together to deliver O2 to muscles and remove CO2.

lessons.title: Aerobic and Anaerobic Exercise
lessons.description: Word equations for energy release, fuel use and how exercise intensity determines the energy system used.
lessons.content_html:
How the Body Releases Energy

All physical activity requires energy. The body releases energy stored in food by breaking down glucose through chemical reactions inside muscle cells. Whether those reactions require oxygen or not determines which energy system is used — and that, in turn, is determined by the intensity and duration of the activity. Understanding the difference between aerobic and anaerobic exercise is fundamental to explaining why a marathon runner can sustain effort for hours while a sprinter is exhausted after ten seconds.

Aerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration occurs when the working muscles have sufficient oxygen to break down glucose completely. The word equation is:

Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

Aerobic respiration produces a large amount of energy (ATP) relative to the amount of glucose used — around 36–38 ATP molecules per glucose. Because the products (carbon dioxide and water) are easily removed from the body via the lungs and sweat, the system can sustain itself for hours without producing harmful waste. It operates at low to moderate intensities: distance running, cycling, swimming, rowing at a steady pace. Mo Farah completing a 10,000 m race relies almost entirely on aerobic respiration for the majority of the race distance.

Aerobic respiration also uses fats (fatty acids) as a fuel source, not just glucose. At lower intensities (e.g. a gentle jog), a larger proportion of energy comes from fat oxidation. As intensity rises, the body shifts progressively towards carbohydrate (glucose/glycogen) as its primary fuel because carbohydrates can be broken down faster. This is why elite endurance athletes train to “fat-adapt” and preserve their limited glycogen stores for higher-intensity surges.

Anaerobic Respiration

Anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen delivery to the muscles cannot keep up with the energy demand. At very high intensities — a 100 m sprint, a maximal weightlifting effort, a final kick at the end of a race — the muscles cannot wait for the cardiovascular system to deliver more oxygen. They switch to producing ATP without oxygen. The word equation is:

Glucose → lactic acid + energy

Anaerobic respiration produces far less energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration (approximately 2 ATP vs 36–38). The by-product is lactic acid. As lactic acid accumulates, it interferes with muscle contraction and causes the burning pain associated with sprinting or performing many press-ups. This is why anaerobic exercise cannot be sustained for long — typically up to about 2 minutes at maximal intensity before performance drops sharply.

Key Fact

Aerobic: glucose + oxygen → CO2 + water + energy. Sustained, large ATP yield, no harmful by-products. Fuel: glucose and fats. Anaerobic: glucose → lactic acid + energy. Fast but limited ATP yield, lactic acid by-product causes fatigue. Fuel: glucose (carbohydrates only).

Intensity, Duration and Energy System Selection

The two energy systems are not switched between like an on/off button — they operate on a continuum based on exercise intensity. At low to moderate intensities, the aerobic system dominates. As intensity increases towards maximum, the anaerobic system contributes more. In most sports, both systems are operating simultaneously, but the balance shifts with each change in pace or effort.

The anaerobic threshold (also called the lactate threshold) is the point at which lactic acid begins to accumulate faster than the body can remove it. Athletes who train regularly can push this threshold higher, sustaining greater intensities aerobically for longer before switching into anaerobic metabolism. This is one of the key benefits of aerobic training.

Consider a 400 m sprint: the first 100–200 m use a mix of aerobic and anaerobic energy. The final 100 m, when fatigue sets in, is heavily anaerobic. A middle-distance 800 m runner relies on both systems — about 60% aerobic, 40% anaerobic. A marathon runner is almost entirely aerobic (95%+). Team sport players cycle repeatedly between aerobic recovery phases and anaerobic sprints, which is why their training must develop both systems.

Key Fact

The critical factor is intensity: low–moderate intensity = aerobic (oxygen sufficient); high intensity = anaerobic (oxygen insufficient). Duration matters too: aerobic systems can last hours; anaerobic systems fatigue within 1–2 minutes. Both operate simultaneously in most sports, with the balance shifting as effort changes.

Students often write “football is aerobic” or “100 m sprint is anaerobic” as if these are complete answers. The mark scheme requires justified reasoning. For the 100 m: “The 100 m sprint lasts approximately 10 seconds at maximal intensity. The demand for energy is so high that the cardiovascular system cannot deliver oxygen fast enough. Muscles therefore rely on anaerobic respiration, producing lactic acid.” For football: “Football involves both aerobic phases (jogging between play, low-intensity possession) and anaerobic phases (sprinting to win a loose ball, accelerating to beat a defender). A midfielder covers around 10 km per match, mostly aerobically, but with approximately 50–100 maximal sprints.” Always anchor your answer to intensity AND duration.

Carbohydrates (glucose, stored as glycogen in muscles and liver) are the body’s preferred fuel because they can be broken down aerobically or anaerobically and produce ATP quickly. Fats (stored in adipose tissue as triglycerides) can only be broken down aerobically and the process is slower. This means fats are the dominant fuel at rest and during light exercise (e.g. walking), but as exercise intensity rises, the body increasingly depends on carbohydrate because it delivers energy faster. Importantly, carbohydrate stores are limited — a typical athlete has around 400–500 g of glycogen available — while fat stores are virtually unlimited. “Hitting the wall” in a marathon refers to glycogen depletion forcing an abrupt shift to fat-dominated metabolism, which cannot sustain marathon pace. This is why carbohydrate fuelling strategies matter in endurance sport.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When justifying whether an activity is aerobic or anaerobic, always reference both intensity and duration — not just one. Exam answers that say “because it’s short” or “because it’s long” without mentioning oxygen availability will lose marks. On Calculate questions involving aerobic/anaerobic thresholds (e.g. calculating target heart rate zones), use the simplified Karvonen formula: aerobic zone = 60–80% of max HR (max HR = 220 − age); anaerobic zone = 80–90% of max HR. Show the full working: max HR first, then the percentage calculation, then state units (bpm).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → CO2 + water + energy. Large ATP yield, sustainable for hours. Fats used at low intensity; carbohydrates dominate at higher intensity.
  • Anaerobic respiration: glucose → lactic acid + energy. Small ATP yield, produces fatigue-causing lactic acid, sustainable only 1–2 minutes.
  • Most sports use both systems simultaneously. The balance is determined by exercise intensity: low–moderate = aerobic dominates; high intensity = anaerobic contributes increasingly. Justify with reference to both intensity and oxygen availability in exam answers.

lessons.title: Short-Term Effects of Exercise
lessons.description: How heart rate, breathing rate, depth and lactate levels change during physical activity.
lessons.content_html:
The Body’s Immediate Response to Exercise

The moment you start exercising, your body begins a coordinated series of adjustments to match the increased energy demand of working muscles. These short-term effects happen within seconds to minutes of activity beginning — and many begin even before you start, as the body anticipates exercise. Understanding what changes, why it changes, and why it matters to a performer is the focus of this lesson.

Heart Rate Response

At rest, heart rate is typically 60–80 beats per minute (bpm). As exercise begins, heart rate rises almost immediately due to signals from the nervous system and hormones such as adrenaline. This anticipatory rise — technically called the anticipatory rise — can increase heart rate even before any physical exertion, as observed in athletes waiting on the start line.

Once exercise is underway, heart rate continues to climb in proportion to intensity. At light intensity, heart rate may stabilise at 100–120 bpm. At moderate intensity (aerobic zone), it sits between 120 and 160 bpm. At maximal intensity (all-out sprinting), heart rate can reach 180–200 bpm. The maximum heart rate is estimated by 220 minus age: a 16-year-old has a maximum of approximately 204 bpm.

The reason for the increase is straightforward: working muscles demand more oxygen. The heart compensates by beating faster, increasing the volume of blood — and therefore oxygen — delivered per minute. Cardiac output rises from roughly 5 litres per minute at rest to over 20 litres per minute during maximal exercise, driven by increases in both heart rate and stroke volume.

Key Fact

Short-term cardiovascular response: heart rate rises immediately due to nervous system signals and adrenaline; anticipatory rise occurs before exercise starts; during exercise, HR increases with intensity; both HR and stroke volume increase, raising cardiac output from ~5 L/min at rest to over 20 L/min at maximal exercise.

Breathing Rate and Depth

Alongside the cardiovascular response, the respiratory system rapidly increases both the rate and depth of breathing. At rest, a typical adult breathes about 12–20 times per minute with a tidal volume of around 0.5 litres. During maximal exercise, breathing rate can rise to 40–60 breaths per minute and tidal volume can reach 3 litres, increasing total air moved per minute (minute ventilation) from roughly 6 L/min at rest to over 100 L/min during maximal exercise.

The increased rate and depth of breathing serves two purposes: it brings more oxygen to the alveoli for gas exchange, and it removes the increased carbon dioxide produced by working muscles. CO2 is a key stimulus for breathing: receptors in the brain and blood vessels detect rising CO2 levels and signal the respiratory centre in the brainstem to increase the rate and depth of breathing automatically.

Both changes (rate and depth) are important. Increasing rate alone would result in shallow breathing with lots of air moving in the trachea and bronchi — the “dead space” that never reaches the alveoli. Increasing depth ensures that each breath reaches the alveoli where gas exchange can actually occur. In well-trained athletes, the body preferentially increases depth rather than rate up to moderate intensities, making breathing more efficient.

Lactate Accumulation

During low to moderate exercise, lactic acid is produced in small amounts and is cleared by the aerobic system as fast as it is made. As intensity increases past the lactate threshold, production exceeds removal and lactic acid begins to accumulate in the muscle and blood. This accumulation has several consequences for the performer: muscles begin to feel heavy and painful; coordination can deteriorate; and the performer must reduce intensity or stop.

For a GCSE performer, understanding lactate accumulation is directly relevant to race strategy and training. A 400 m runner who goes out too fast will exceed their lactate threshold early, accumulating lactic acid that impairs their ability to maintain speed in the final straight. A well-trained distance runner has a higher lactate threshold, meaning they can run faster before lactic acid begins to accumulate — one of the key benefits of regular aerobic training.

Muscle fatigue during intense exercise is partly caused by lactic acid accumulation and partly by the depletion of energy stores (particularly glycogen). After exercise ends, breathing rate remains elevated for a period — this is the excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC), sometimes called oxygen debt. During this recovery phase, oxygen is used to break down lactic acid, restore muscle glycogen, replenish the oxygen stores in haemoglobin and myoglobin, and return body temperature and heart rate to resting values.

Key Fact

Three key short-term effects: (1) Heart rate and cardiac output increase — to deliver more oxygen to working muscles. (2) Breathing rate and depth increase — to supply more oxygen to alveoli and remove more CO2. (3) Lactate accumulates if intensity exceeds the lactate threshold — causing muscle fatigue and a limit on sustained high-intensity effort.

Heart rate is not the only cardiovascular adjustment during exercise. Stroke volume also increases. As muscles contract during exercise, they squeeze the veins running through them (the “muscle pump”), propelling blood back to the heart faster. This increased venous return stretches the ventricles and causes them to contract more forcefully (Starling’s law of the heart), ejecting more blood per beat. At rest, stroke volume is around 70 ml; during exercise, it can rise to 110–130 ml in a trained person. The combined effect of increased HR and increased SV dramatically multiplies cardiac output and oxygen delivery.

Data questions often present a graph or table of heart rate, stroke volume or cardiac output at rest and during exercise. To score full marks on an interpret data question, you need to: (1) quote a specific figure from the data with units (e.g. “heart rate rose from 72 bpm to 168 bpm”); (2) identify the trend (rising, plateauing, falling); and (3) link the trend to a physiological reason or sporting implication (e.g. “the rise in HR increases cardiac output, ensuring more oxygen reaches the working leg muscles during the running phase”). Students who only quote a figure without explaining its significance, or who explain the physiology without quoting data, typically score half marks.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On data interpretation questions about heart rate or cardiac output, the mark scheme expects three elements: a figure quoted from the data with units, a trend statement, and a physiological explanation. Missing any one of these costs marks. On Explain questions about short-term effects, use the chain ‘what changes → why → consequence for performance.’ For lactate accumulation: ‘lactic acid accumulates (what) because intensity exceeds the lactate threshold and anaerobic respiration rate outpaces removal (why), causing muscle fatigue and forcing the performer to slow down (consequence).’ On Calculate questions, always show the formula (Q = SV × HR), substitute the values, and give units (ml/min or L/min).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Short-term cardiovascular responses to exercise: heart rate and stroke volume both increase, raising cardiac output from ~5 L/min at rest to 20+ L/min; anticipatory rise occurs before exercise begins due to adrenaline and nervous system signals.
  • Short-term respiratory responses: breathing rate rises (12–20 to 40–60 breaths/min) and tidal volume increases (~0.5 to ~3 L), increasing minute ventilation to supply more O2 and remove more CO2.
  • Lactate accumulates when exercise intensity exceeds the lactate threshold; this causes muscle fatigue. EPOC (oxygen debt) after exercise clears lactic acid and restores the body to its resting state.

lessons.title: Long-Term Effects of Training
lessons.description: Adaptations to the body systems from sustained training, including hypertrophy and resting heart rate changes.
lessons.content_html:
How the Body Adapts to Regular Training

Short-term effects of exercise disappear within minutes to hours of activity ending. Long-term effects, by contrast, are permanent structural and functional changes that build up over weeks and months of regular training. These adaptations are what transform a novice into a trained athlete — they increase the body’s capacity to perform, recover and handle greater training loads. Understanding long-term adaptations allows you to explain why Adam Peaty or Beth Mead can perform at intensities that would exhaust an untrained person.

Long-term adaptations occur across two systems: the musculo-skeletal system (muscles, bones, ligaments and tendons) and the cardio-respiratory system (heart, lungs and blood vessels). Both systems adapt together with regular aerobic and resistance training, but the specific adaptations differ by training type and intensity.

Musculo-Skeletal Adaptations

Muscle hypertrophy is the most visible long-term adaptation to resistance training. When muscles are subjected to repeated overload — lifting weights progressively heavier than they are accustomed to — the individual muscle fibres increase in diameter. This is caused by an increase in the number and thickness of the contractile proteins (actin and myosin) within each fibre. Hypertrophy increases the muscle’s cross-sectional area and therefore its force production capacity. It is most pronounced in Type II fibres (particularly Type IIx) and occurs most rapidly with resistance training programmes that use high loads and moderate to high volume.

However, it is important to note that hypertrophy requires adequate rest. Muscle fibres are damaged by intense training, and the repair and growth process — mediated by satellite cells — occurs during rest periods, not during the training session itself. Without sufficient recovery time between sessions, the body cannot complete the repair process, and performance may decline rather than improve. This is why rest is programmed into training plans as a component of progressive overload.

Regular weight-bearing training also increases bone density. Mechanical loading stimulates bone-forming cells (osteoblasts) to deposit calcium and phosphorus, increasing the mineral content of the bone matrix. Increased bone density reduces the risk of stress fractures during training and osteoporosis in later life — a particularly important benefit for young female athletes who may be at risk of low bone density due to insufficient calorie intake.

Ligaments and tendons also adapt to training: they increase in strength and thickness with regular loading, becoming more resistant to sprain and rupture. This is why a well-conditioned athlete is less likely to suffer a ligament injury than a sedentary individual doing the same activity. Tendons also increase in stiffness, which can improve the efficiency with which they transmit force from muscle to bone — beneficial in running economy and jumping performance.

Key Fact

Musculo-skeletal long-term adaptations: muscle hypertrophy (stronger, larger muscle fibres), increased bone density (calcium/phosphorus deposition), stronger ligaments and tendons (resist injury better). All require progressive overload and adequate rest to occur. Hypertrophy is most pronounced in Type II fibres; bone density increases most from weight-bearing exercise.

Cardio-Respiratory Adaptations

The heart responds to sustained aerobic training by becoming larger and stronger, a phenomenon called cardiac hypertrophy. Specifically, the left ventricle increases in size, allowing it to hold and eject a greater volume of blood per beat — an increase in resting stroke volume. This is the structural foundation for two of the most important training adaptations: bradycardia (a lower resting heart rate) and a faster recovery heart rate after exercise.

The mechanism is elegant: because the trained heart ejects more blood per beat (higher resting SV, up to 100+ ml vs ~70 ml in untrained), it needs to beat fewer times per minute to maintain the same cardiac output at rest. Elite endurance athletes such as distance cyclists or marathon runners can have resting heart rates of 40–50 bpm or even lower, compared to the untrained average of 60–80 bpm. This bradycardia also means the heart has more time between beats to fill and recover, reducing the long-term stress on the cardiac muscle.

Faster recovery after exercise is another measurable adaptation. A trained athlete’s heart rate returns to resting values much more quickly after a bout of exercise than that of an untrained person. This is partly because their higher resting SV means the cardiovascular system achieves adequate oxygen delivery even at lower heart rates.

Key Fact

Cardio-respiratory adaptation chain: aerobic training → cardiac hypertrophy (larger left ventricle) → higher resting stroke volume → bradycardia (lower resting HR), faster recovery HR, higher maximum cardiac output. The same cardiac output can be maintained at a lower heart rate, reducing cardiac strain and extending sustainable exercise duration.

Blood and circulation also adapt. Training increases the total number of red blood cells, boosting the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. Capillary networks become denser around muscle fibres — a process called capillarisation. More capillaries means oxygen and nutrients can diffuse into muscle fibres more rapidly, and lactic acid and CO2 can be removed more efficiently. Resting blood pressure tends to decrease with aerobic training, because the blood vessel walls become more elastic.

In the lungs, training increases lung capacity and vital capacity, and strengthens the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles. More alveoli may become functional with training, increasing the total surface area available for gas exchange. These adaptations collectively allow a trained athlete to take in and use oxygen at a far greater rate than an untrained person — quantified by the measure VO2 max, the maximum volume of oxygen that can be consumed per minute.

Training is a stimulus, not an adaptation. The adaptation — muscle fibre repair and growth, increased bone mineral density, capillarisation — happens during rest, not during the training session. A session that overloads the muscle is only beneficial if the body is given sufficient time to repair and over-compensate (supercompensation). This is the physiological basis of the principle of rest and recovery within progressive overload. Over-training without adequate rest leads to persistent muscle damage, reduced immune function, and declining performance — a condition called overtraining syndrome. Well-designed training programmes periodise rest days and lighter weeks to allow the body to adapt fully before the next overload stimulus is applied.

Long-term adaptations are not permanent. When training stops (due to injury, illness or lifestyle change), the body begins to reverse its adaptations — a principle called reversibility. Cardiovascular adaptations are lost relatively quickly: resting heart rate rises within weeks as stroke volume decreases; capillary density reduces. Muscle hypertrophy is lost more slowly, but sustained inactivity leads to significant muscle atrophy. Bone density adaptations persist longer than cardiovascular adaptations because bone remodelling is a slow process. For returning athletes after injury, this is a key reason why maintaining some form of low-impact activity (e.g. pool running, upper-body gym work) during recovery is better than complete rest where possible.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On Explain questions about long-term adaptations, always state the adaptation, the mechanism (why it occurs) and the performance benefit. Writing ‘the heart gets bigger’ earns one mark; ‘cardiac hypertrophy increases the volume of the left ventricle, which raises resting stroke volume, so the heart can maintain cardiac output at a lower heart rate (bradycardia), reducing cardiac strain and extending endurance performance’ earns full marks. On 9-mark Evaluate questions, draw on both musculo-skeletal and cardio-respiratory adaptations — examiners reward breadth and the ability to link adaptations back to specific sport performance improvements. Always include rest and reversibility as limiting conditions to show nuanced understanding.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Musculo-skeletal long-term adaptations: muscle hypertrophy (increased fibre size and strength), increased bone density, stronger ligaments and tendons. All require progressive overload and adequate rest.
  • Cardio-respiratory long-term adaptations: cardiac hypertrophy → higher stroke volume → bradycardia (lower resting HR) and faster recovery; capillarisation, more red blood cells, reduced resting blood pressure, increased lung capacity and vital capacity.
  • Adaptations require rest to develop (supercompensation principle) and are reversible: stopping training causes the body to return towards its pre-training state, with cardiovascular adaptations lost faster than structural musculo-skeletal ones.
